chief_complaint: nightmares and avoidance of highways 8 months post-crash
hpi_details: A 47-year-old male presents to the clinic with nightmares and avoidance of highways 8 months post-crash. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: He thinks the violent impact of the car collision physically scrambled his nervous system and trapped his brain in constant shock.
concerns: He is worried that having a sudden panic freeze behind the wheel will cause another catastrophic highway pileup.
expectations: He hopes to get medication to suppress the terrifying night terrors so he can sleep through the night without waking up screaming.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes trauma-focused psychotherapy; medication options for comorbid symptoms or nightmares require individualized clinician assessment and monitoring.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: nightmares and avoidance of highways 8 months post-crash

Key HPI features: A 47-year-old male presents to the clinic with nightmares and avoidance of highways 8 months post-crash. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
Objective/Exam findings: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Adjustment disorder without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Acute suicidal or homicidal ideation.
management_principles: Offer trauma-focused psychotherapy when clinically appropriate.
A qualified prescriber may consider and monitor medication for target symptoms after reviewing contraindications and adverse effects.
Assess self-harm, violence, and acute safety risk; arrange urgent psychiatric evaluation when risk is imminent.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

must_ask.say: Can you tell me what happened in the crash and how you felt afterward?
Do you have nightmares or flashbacks about the crash?
Have you avoided driving or highways since the accident?
Do you feel jumpy, on edge, or startle easily?
Have you had thoughts of harming yourself, and how has this affected your daily life?

history.answer: Ever since a bad car crash eight months ago, I keep having vivid nightmares and I am terrified of driving on the highway.
Eight months ago, another car merged right into my lane at high speed and spun me into the concrete barrier. My car was completely totaled, and I honestly thought I was going to die.
Right after the accident I felt shaken up, but over the past two months the nightmares and highway fear have become much more intense. It feels like it is steadily getting worse.
My anxiety flares up specifically whenever I have to drive or get anywhere near high-speed roads. Outside of those situations, I feel more on edge than anxious.
I do not have sudden panic attacks that come out of nowhere and peak in ten minutes. The intense panic only hits when I am forced to drive near highway ramps or wake up from a bad dream.
When I get close to the highway, my heart pounds, my chest feels constricted, and my hands start trembling. Once I turn away onto a local road, those feelings slowly settle down.
I completely avoid driving on highways and take backroads everywhere, which adds forty minutes to my commute. Some days I even avoid driving entirely if the roads look crowded.
Almost every night I wake up in a cold sweat reliving the sound of the metal crushing. During the daytime, if I hear tires screeching or horns blowing, the entire collision replays in my mind.
I feel like I am always on guard and scanning other drivers constantly. Any sudden loud noise makes me jump right out of my chair.
I dread going to bed because of the nightmares, so I only sleep about three or four broken hours a night. Because of that, I feel completely exhausted throughout the day.
My neck and shoulder muscles feel tight all the time. I also notice I get annoyed and snap at small frustrations easily because my nerves are so frayed.
I have no problem speaking in meetings or interacting with colleagues at work. My fear is strictly tied to driving and the crash.
My commute takes twice as long, so I am constantly late or exhausted at work. It has also made me irritable with my family at home.
Other than the stress from the accident and my difficult daily commute, my job and home finances have been stable.
I feel drained and worn out from not sleeping, but I do not feel hopeless or like life is not worth living.
No, I have never had any thoughts of hurting myself or ending my life. I really want to overcome this and get back to normal.
I still shower, brush my teeth, and eat three meals a day, even though I feel tired most of the afternoon.
I was wearing my seatbelt and the airbag deployed, but I did not lose consciousness or strike my head. I have not had chronic headaches, dizziness, or memory gaps since then.
No, I have not had any heat intolerance, unexplained weight loss, or unusual sweating during the day.
No, I have never experienced chest pain during physical exercise, and I have never passed out.
I just drink one standard cup of brewed black coffee each morning to stay awake at work. I do not drink energy drinks.
I have a beer or two with dinner on weekends, but that is all. I do not take sleeping pills, tranquilizers, or any recreational drugs.
I tried listening to quiet audiobooks and taking deep breaths behind the wheel, but my hands still shake when traffic speeds up. I have not seen a doctor or counselor for this yet.
I think the sheer shock and impact of that wreck permanently damaged my nerves and left me stuck in survival mode.
I'm terrified that if I try to take the highway, I'll freeze at the wheel and cause another terrible pileup.
I'm hoping you can give me something to stop these horrible nightmares so I don't keep waking up in a sweat every single night.
I have always been healthy and have never been diagnosed with high blood pressure, diabetes, or heart problems.
Right after the accident eight months ago, I was checked at the emergency room and cleared without any fractures or overnight stays. I have never had surgery.
I do not take any daily prescription medications, over-the-counter medicines, or herbal remedies.
I do not have any allergies to medications, foods, or latex.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any tobacco or vaping products.
Nobody in my immediate family has a history of anxiety disorders, depression, or other mental health conditions.
I work as an operations coordinator at a local supply company, and I live with my wife and our teenage son in a single-family house.

exam.finding: Blood pressure is 122/78 mmHg, heart rate is 76 beats per minute, respiratory rate is 16 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation is 99% on room air, and body temperature is 36.8 degrees Celsius.
Alert, well-groomed male who appears mildly fatigued and apprehensive, but is in no acute physical distress.
Fully oriented to person, place, and time; speech is fluent and regular, thought process is logical and coherent, and affect is anxious when discussing the motor vehicle collision.
Pupils are equal, round, and reactive to light; no proptosis, lid lag, or abnormal extraocular movements.
Thyroid gland is normal in size, smooth, and non-tender without palpable nodules or bruits.
No resting, postural, or kinetic tremor observed in either outstretched hand.
Regular rate and rhythm with normal S1 and S2; no murmurs, gallops, or friction rubs.
Clear breath sounds bilaterally without wheezing, crackles, or rhonchi.
Cranial nerves II through XII are grossly intact with symmetric facial movements and intact sensation.
